title: Host — eq12 (Beelink EQ12, N100)
description: Everything observable on the eq12 chassis: power, thermals, fan speed, CPU, memory, network and storage. Metrics come from the native telegraf agent on the Proxmox host (#186), its RAPL exec input (#194) and the forced it87 binding that makes this board's fan tachometers readable. Guest-internal metrics live under host="eq12_docker" and are not on this dashboard — this is the physical machine.

panels.title: Uptime
panels.description: Time since last boot (`system_uptime`).

panels.title: Load (1m)
panels.description: 1-minute run-queue length. This host has 4 logical CPUs, so sustained load above that means work is queueing rather than running.

panels.title: CPU busy
panels.description: 100 minus idle, across all cores.

panels.title: Memory used
panels.description: Of 16 GiB total.

panels.title: Package power
panels.description: CPU package power from the RAPL energy counter. THIS IS NOT WALL POWER: it excludes NVMe, fans, the PSU's conversion loss and everything else on the board, and there is no wall meter on this machine.

panels.title: Hottest sensor
panels.description: Maximum across every temperature reading on the board, whatever chip it came from. Use the Thermals row to see which one it is.

panels.title: Chassis fan
panels.description: Fan 2, the faster of this board's two tachometers. Readable only because the stock it87 driver is force-bound to a chip it does not recognise by name (see docs/eq12.md).

panels.title: Root filesystem
panels.description: Usage of `/`.

panels.title: CPU power by RAPL domain
panels.description: All three domains this N100 exposes. `core` HERE IS A GENUINE ALL-CORE AGGREGATE — established by a load-placement test that disqualified n5pro's identically-named domain, because coverage is a property of the board and never of the name (#194). `package-0` is the sum the chassis actually draws for the SoC; `uncore` is the iGPU and fabric, and reads essentially zero at idle, which is correct and not a broken sensor.

panels.title: Package power — 7 day trend
panels.description: Pinned to a 7-day window regardless of the dashboard's time range, so a slow upward drift in idle draw is visible without changing anything. Min and max in the legend are the useful numbers here, not the last value.

panels.title: Every temperature sensor
panels.description: One series per chip/feature pair reported by lm-sensors. The chip tag is what disambiguates identically-named features across different chips.

panels.title: NVMe (SMART)
panels.description: Drive-reported composite temperature from smartctl, which is a different sensor path from the `nvme-pci-*` hwmon chip above — they should track, and a divergence is interesting.

panels.title: Fan speed
panels.description: Two real tachometers on the it8622 Super-I/O chip. If these go flat at zero while temperatures climb, that is the failure this panel exists to catch. If they disappear entirely, the forced it87 binding did not survive a boot — docs/eq12.md records that this is inferred rather than measured.

panels.title: Fan PWM duty
panels.description: Commanded duty cycle, 0-255, for the five PWM channels the chip exposes. Only two have tachometers attached, so a channel moving here with no matching RPM change is either an unpopulated header or a fan with no tacho wire. Deliberately a SEPARATE panel from RPM rather than a second axis on the same one.

panels.title: ACPI cooling-device state
panels.description: The firmware's own cooling-device objects. All five read 0 on this board and always have — they are kept because their DISAPPEARANCE is a meaningful signal (#202), not because the value is informative. Fan speed above is the real measurement.

panels.title: CPU time by mode
panels.description: Stacked to 100%. `iowait` climbing means the CPU is waiting on storage, not busy; `steal` is only meaningful under virtualisation.

panels.title: Load average
panels.description: 1 / 5 / 15 minute run-queue length. The dashed reference is 4 logical CPUs.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: `used` excludes cache and buffers. On a ZFS host a large slab/ARC is normal and is not a leak.

panels.title: Swap and processes
panels.description: Swap in/out rate is the signal that matters — a large swap *used* with zero rate is just cold pages.

panels.title: Physical NIC throughput
panels.description: This board has two 2.5GbE ports (`enp1s0`, `enp2s0`). Only `enp2s0` is cabled, and it is negotiated at 1000 Mb/s rather than 2500 — see the link-speed table. `vmbr0` is the bridge carrying guest traffic over it.

panels.title: Errors and drops
panels.description: Both should be flat at zero. A non-zero rate here is a cable, a duplex mismatch, or a saturated ring buffer — it will show up as latency long before it shows up as an outage.

panels.title: Guest interface throughput
panels.description: Per-guest taps and veths, which is how you attribute host network load to a particular VM or container.

panels.title: Link speed
panels.description: Negotiated link speed in Mb/s. `enp2s0` reads 1000 on a 2.5GbE port, which is a property of the switch port or the cable run, not of the NIC. An interface that is down reports no series at all rather than 0.

panels.title: Disk throughput
panels.description: Whole devices only — partitions are excluded so the same bytes are not counted twice.

panels.title: Disk utilisation and latency
panels.description: `io_util` is the fraction of wall time the device had a request in flight. Sustained 100% means the device is the bottleneck.

panels.title: Filesystem usage
panels.description: ZFS datasets and the root filesystem.

panels.title: NVMe health (SMART)
panels.description: `health_ok` is smartctl's overall verdict: 1 is passing. `percentage_used` is the drive's own wear estimate — it can exceed 100 and is not a capacity figure. `available_spare` falling toward its threshold is the number that predicts failure.
